title: Two Parties

jokes.text: Water? Like fire water? That's racist, and I do not appreciate it. / I'm just messing with you.
jokes.setup: Leslie offers Ken water as polite hospitality; Ken responds with 'Like fire water?' implying Leslie is being racist, making Leslie immediately panic and apologize
jokes.punchline: Ken reveals he's just messing with her — the accusation was a deliberate joke at Leslie's expense
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly efficient cold open joke. Ken weaponizes white liberal guilt with perfect comedic precision — the setup is completely innocent, Leslie's panic is entirely earned, and the punchline reframes Ken as a sharp, self-aware trickster rather than a victim. The joke is deeply character-integrated: this specific dynamic (progressive white woman stepping on cultural landmines) is exactly what makes Ken Hotate work as a character. High rewatch value because you hear the joke differently knowing what Ken is doing.

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: Fire water? Yes, I'll take some fire water.

jokes.text: He does that sometimes.
jokes.setup: Ken's 'fire water' trick has visibly flustered everyone in the room
jokes.punchline: Leslie's casual, almost-resigned acknowledgment that this is a known pattern — delivered as though it's the most normal thing in the world
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economic follow-up. Four words that tell us Leslie has a history with Ken's pranks, deepens his characterization retroactively, and gets the laugh through total understatement. The best possible button on Joke 1.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Wait, you were joking?

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: Of course I was joking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Ha ha ha, that's great, that's great.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh wow, we were so worried.

jokes.text: But seriously. I'll have a whiskey.
jokes.setup: The room is still processing Ken's joke when he pivots
jokes.punchline: 'But seriously' implies depth of wisdom or a correction — then it's just a drink order, delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: Ken's comic voice is fully established in this moment. The 'but seriously' transition is a classic setup for a meaningful pivot — subverting it with a drink order is elegant and characterful. It also lightly echoes the fire water setup, adding a tiny layer of meta-commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: You know what? I do want alcohol. So your question wasn't entirely off-base.

jokes.text: Talking head: describing Pawnee's historically 'murder-y' relationship with the Wamapoke
jokes.setup: Leslie sets up a formally diplomatic description of Pawnee's historical relationship with the Wamapoke, pausing dramatically
jokes.punchline: The single word 'Murder-y' — a casual, made-up adjective — used to describe genocide
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy of language. The buildup of formal diplomatic framing followed by '...murder-y' is a textbook Parks and Rec structure — the show's whole ethos of optimistic people dealing with a deeply flawed history compressed into one invented word. Highly quotable, very specific to this world. The casual suffix '-y' applied to murder is the entire joke and it lands perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Look, the historical relationship between Pawnee and the Wamapoke tribe is... well, it's not great. There was a lot of, um, murder-y stuff that happened.

jokes.text: "Our slots are downright filthy." I think it's a slam-dunk idea. I think we're done here.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to diplomatically navigate casino advertising in a public park; Ken proposes a slogan
jokes.punchline: The slogan is gleefully inappropriate for a public park setting, and Leslie's 'I think we're done here' is both a straight reaction and an acknowledgment of how badly this is going
jokes.explanation: The slogan joke works on two levels: as pure absurdist humor (a casino slogan that sounds pornographic) and as character comedy (Ken lording it over the hapless Leslie). Leslie's instant 'I think we're done here' is a great straight-man button. Solid, funny, well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: Our new casino slogan is 'Come for the slots, stay for the slots.'

jokes.text: Is he joking? / I don't know.
jokes.setup: Ken suggests retiring to his 'longhouse' to 'smoke the ceremonial peace pipe to celebrate' — which could be sincere, sarcastic, or another prank
jokes.punchline: The shared bewilderment between Leslie and her colleague — they genuinely cannot tell — is the joke. Ken's inscrutable trickster persona has completely destabilized them.
jokes.explanation: A nice button on the opening Ken Hotate sequence. The joke is the uncertainty itself — Ken has successfully established that nobody can read him, and this beat pays that off efficiently. Not a huge laugh but a satisfying scene-ender.

jokes.text: anything that can be penis-shaped will be penis-shaped
jokes.setup: Ann lists the amenities of the bachelorette party — dancing, Jell-o shots, karaoke — in a straight run of normal party activities
jokes.punchline: The final item breaks the pattern with gleeful, categorical commitment to a single theme
jokes.explanation: A reliable bachelorette party joke — not original in concept but well-structured as a list punchline. The absolute categorical phrasing ('anything that CAN be') gives it slightly more punch than a simpler version. It's a functional crowd-pleaser.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: I have a longhouse.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: A longhouse?

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: Yes, a longhouse. It's a traditional Native American dwelling.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Ken, are you serious right now?

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: Completely serious.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I genuinely cannot tell if he's joking.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Yeah, like, is this a thing? Does Ken have a longhouse?

jokes.text: Which is why I'm stress-eating gummy penises.
jokes.setup: Ann explains in a talking head that she needs Leslie's bachelorette party to go well, and is clearly anxious about it
jokes.punchline: The camera reveals (implied) that she is literally stress-eating gummy penis candies while delivering this sincere confessional — the visual contradicts the earnestness
jokes.explanation: The callback to the penis-shape theme works perfectly here — Ann is literally living the bachelorette experience while confessing her stress. The juxtaposition of 'stress-eating' (a sincere emotional behavior) with 'gummy penises' (absurd object) is efficient and funny. Good visual gag for a mockumentary format.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: So for my bachelorette party, we're going to have penis-shaped straws, penis-shaped cake, penis-shaped balloons, penis-shaped napkins, penis-shaped plates, penis-shaped cups, penis-shaped centerpieces, and a penis piñata.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ann, that's amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: It's not amazing, Leslie. It's a nightmare. I just wanted a nice, tasteful party and somehow we ended up with a penis explosion.

jokes.text: Jerry forced his way in there somehow--things are bound to get crazy. The game is Settlers of Catan.
jokes.setup: Ben's talking head hypes the bachelor party guest list — Haverford, Swanson, Dwyer — building toward an expectation of debauchery, especially after noting 'Jerry forced his way in'
jokes.punchline: Cut to the game being Settlers of Catan. The buildup promised mayhem; reality is a board game.
jokes.explanation: A textbook misdirection joke executed with perfect structural awareness. The episode spends real time building a bachelor party expectation ('things are bound to get crazy'), then cuts hard to the anti-climactic truth. What elevates it above a generic subversion is that it's COMPLETELY in character for Ben — the loveable nerd who thinks board games are a peak celebration. The 'The game is Settlers of Catan' delivery as its own sentence, flat and final, is inspired. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: This bachelorette party is literally the most important thing I've ever planned. It's going to be perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie deserves the best night of her life.

jokes.text: I can't believe this is what you want to do for your bachelor party. / Look, guys, we don't have to play this game if you don't want to. I mean, I'm nationally ranked, so it isn't even really fair.
jokes.setup: Tom expresses disbelief at the Settlers of Catan bachelor party; Ben offers to pivot out of politeness
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately undermines his own generous offer by revealing he's nationally ranked — suggesting he actually DOES want to play and would win anyway
jokes.explanation: This joke does double character work simultaneously: it establishes that Ben is EXACTLY the kind of person who would be nationally ranked at Settlers of Catan, AND that his 'we don't have to play' is completely disingenuous. The self-sabotage of his own magnanimous offer is the comedic engine. 'I'm nationally ranked, so it isn't even really fair' is a quotable line that perfectly captures Ben's particular brand of earnest nerdery. Comparable in craft to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: It's just a board game

jokes.text: I'm not a big bachelor party kind of guy, so when the guys asked me what my perfect night would be, I told them the truth-- beer and board games. They thought I was kidding. I was not kidding.
jokes.setup: Ben explains in a talking head his vision for his bachelor party
jokes.punchline: 'They thought I was kidding. I was not kidding.' — the absolute sincerity of Ben's nerddom, communicated with total self-awareness and zero shame
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of 'They thought I was kidding. I was not kidding.' is almost perfectly constructed — the two-sentence structure with identical syntax creates a comedic punch through sheer repetition and finality. It's pure Ben Wyatt. The joke rewards fans who've tracked Ben's nerd characterization across seasons. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I know this is nerdy. I can put on something else if you want.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: No, no, keep going.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Really? Because I have to warn you, I'm actually really good at this.

jokes.text: Is this gonna be one of those cool bachelorette parties where things get out of control and we murder someone, and then we all have to take a blood oath to never reveal our secret? / No. / Then I might have to leave early.
jokes.setup: April arrives at the bachelorette party and frames her participation in terms of what's at stake
jokes.punchline: April's 'cool bachelorette party' involves murder and blood oaths; when told no, she casually threatens to leave — treating murder as a perfectly reasonable party amenity
jokes.explanation: A defining April Ludgate joke. The premise — that a 'cool bachelorette party' involves murder — is perfectly absurdist, but what makes it exceptional is the structure: the specificity ('blood oath to never reveal our secret') suggests April has a detailed vision of this party, and her deadpan threat to leave when murder isn't confirmed is completely in character. The joke is organic to April and couldn't be delivered by any other Parks character. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: So what kind of bachelorette party are we talking about here?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh, just a cool party. Nothing crazy.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Cool party? Leslie, the last time you threw a 'cool party' three people went to the hospital and we all had to sign blood oaths to never speak of it again.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That was one time!

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: It was two times. And one of them involved an actual murder.

jokes.text: Well, well, well. Don't you ladies look nice... For once? Just kidding. I've actually always been attracted to this one.
jokes.setup: Jamm arrives unexpectedly at the bachelorette party location, which turns out to be the development site he's stealing
jokes.punchline: Jamm's sleazy compliment-insult-recovery sequence, ending with singling out one woman as an object of attraction — classic Jamm as an avatar of gross male behavior
jokes.explanation: Functional Jamm cringe comedy. The sequence (compliment → backhanded insult → 'just kidding' → creepy attraction declaration) is well-paced and in character for Jamm as a sleazy antagonist. But there's no genuine surprise or craft innovation — it's exactly what you'd expect Jamm to say. Does its job without distinction.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: So you're telling me there's no murder at this party?

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Well, that's disappointing.

jokes.text: "Future home of Paunch Burger. Start drooling, fatties"
jokes.setup: Leslie reads the sign Jamm has already erected on the development site
jokes.punchline: The sign's slogan 'Start drooling, fatties' — an aggressively anti-customer piece of advertising copy that only Jamm's specific brand of gleeful crudeness could produce
jokes.explanation: The Paunch Burger slogan is a recurring piece of the show's satirical universe, and 'Start drooling, fatties' is a good entry — it captures exactly the kind of aggressively contemptuous fast food marketing the show lampoons. The economy is excellent (five words that perfectly characterize the brand). Doesn't break new ground but executes well.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You know, I have to say, you ladies are looking particularly attractive today. I mean, for women.

jokes.text: Turns out, I don't care. / You can't stop this train.
jokes.setup: Leslie points out the deal still has two weeks left; Jamm acknowledges this is true
jokes.punchline: 'Turns out, I don't care.' — the frank admission that rules simply don't apply to him, delivered without a hint of shame
jokes.explanation: Jamm's shamelessness is his comedic superpower, and this line captures it efficiently. 'Turns out, I don't care' has the structure of a logical conclusion reached through deliberation — as if Jamm weighed the rules and found them wanting. Good economy, strong character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: What I meant to say is... I have nothing against women in the workplace. Some of my best friends are women. In fact, I'm very progressive. I even let my wife have her own credit card.

jokes.text: Aw, sweet! A new Paunch Burger. Their burgers will kill you! They're full of wasps! Yeah, but they taste real good. Yes, they do, sir.
jokes.setup: A random citizen overhears the Paunch Burger sign; Leslie tries to warn him against it
jokes.punchline: The citizen acknowledges the wasps kill you but finds the taste worth it — and Leslie, exhausted, can only agree
jokes.explanation: This rapid-fire exchange is a gem. The wasps detail is perfectly absurdist — it's not just 'unhealthy,' it's literally full of wasps, suggesting the burger might actively sting you to death. The citizen's philosophical acceptance ('Yeah, but they taste real good') is great, but Leslie's defeated 'Yes, they do, sir' — confirming the wasp burgers taste good — is the real punchline. She can't help herself. The whole exchange takes about five seconds and earns every bit of its laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Welcome to Paunch Burger. Where we don't care about your business, we just want your money. And you're fat.

jokes.text: Seven contiguous segments, giving me longest road and a sweet-ass ten points for the win. Oh, booyah!
jokes.setup: Ben has been playing Settlers of Catan at his own bachelor party
jokes.punchline: Ben's absolute joy at winning his board game — the specificity of 'contiguous segments' and 'longest road' combined with the triumphant 'booyah' reveals a man in his happiest element
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the specificity — a man at his own bachelor party who is this excited to explain his winning Catan strategy. 'Sweet-ass ten points' is a great collision of frat vocabulary with board game nerdery. The 'booyah' is perfectly incongruous. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You don't want to eat at Paunch Burger. Their food is really unhealthy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Actually, it's worse than unhealthy. I'm pretty sure it's filled with insects.

jokes.text: To our new Lord of Catan, Ben Wyatt, a great friend and a wonderful man.
jokes.setup: Chris is giving an earnest, sincere toast to Ben at his bachelor party
jokes.punchline: 'Lord of Catan' — Chris is so committed to sincerity that he treats Ben's board game victory as a genuine title of honor, which is both sweet and absurd
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Chris's complete sincerity. Any other character might be mocking Ben with 'Lord of Catan,' but Chris means it as an actual honorific. It's a perfect expression of both characters simultaneously — Ben's nerdy achievement and Chris's earnest supportiveness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: These burgers could be filled with wasps and nobody would care.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown citizen
dialogue.line: Yeah, probably.

jokes.text: I cannot stand idly by and watch a bachelor party peter out like this. Now, I know you said no strippers 'cause they make you sad. Correct.
jokes.setup: Tom is rallying the group to escalate the bachelor party beyond board games
jokes.punchline: Ben's matter-of-fact 'Correct' confirmation that strippers make him sad — delivered without any embarrassment or elaboration
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in Ben's delivery of 'Correct.' He doesn't qualify, explain, or apologize for the fact that strippers make him sad — he simply confirms it as established fact, like acknowledging his shoe size. It's a beautifully dry acknowledgment of an eccentric personal trait. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You know, I'm actually in an open marriage. My wife and I have an understanding.

jokes.text: Son, there's no wrong way to consume alcohol.
jokes.setup: Tom explains molecular mixology as 'an experimental new way to consume alcohol'
jokes.punchline: Ron's absolute philosophical certainty that alcohol delivery method is irrelevant — all methods are valid — delivered as paternal wisdom
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson philosophy condensed to ten words. The joke works because Ron delivers it with total paternal gravity — 'Son' establishes the register — and because it's both funny AND reveals his character (Ron is ideologically committed to the validity of all alcohol consumption). It's also unexpectedly open-minded for Ron, which is the twist. Highly quotable. Matches the 8.0 anchor in craft and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I'm going to build a settlement here, which gives me two victory points and access to three different resources.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! I rolled a seven! Everyone has to disband their armies! This is the best day of my life!

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Did you see that? I just got the longest road! The LONGEST ROAD! That's fifteen points of continuous pathway mastery!

jokes.text: Here's your Bud Light. / I ordered a beer. / That is a beer.
jokes.setup: Ron has just proclaimed there's no wrong way to consume alcohol; the bar serves molecular cocktails — implying everything will be experimental
jokes.punchline: Ron's order arrives as a completely normal Bud Light in a can, and the bartender's 'That is a beer' is a flat refutation of Ron's implied complaint — Ron's simplicity has defeated the bar's pretensions
jokes.explanation: The joke perfectly caps Ron's speech — the man who said 'there's no wrong way to consume alcohol' immediately objects to his beer, only to be shut down by the bartender's deadpan literalism. It's also a great visual gag: in a bar of fog clouds and martini glasses, Ron gets a can of Bud Light. The specificity of Bud Light (not a craft beer, not a whiskey) is ideal for Ron's character. Excellent structural callback.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: We could have strippers at the bachelor party.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: No strippers. Leslie would kill me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Come on, Ben. It's your bachelor party. Live a little.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I'm serious, Tom. Leslie has made it very clear that if there are strippers, she will end me. And not in a fun way.

jokes.text: May I go ahead and chisel your aromasphere? / Please!
jokes.setup: The bartender serves a 'Nimbus Martini' — a cocktail served as a cloud of fog — and offers to enhance it
jokes.punchline: Jerry's enthusiastic 'Please!' in response to 'chiseling his aromasphere' — Jerry is delighted by the pretentious molecular bar and doesn't question the nonsense phrase
jokes.explanation: The invented bartender jargon 'aromasphere' is good absurdist comedy — it sounds plausible enough to be real molecular mixology speak, which makes it funnier. Jerry's uncritical enthusiasm is a nice character touch — he's the one person who's just happy to be included and experiencing something new.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Tom, I understand you've been experimenting with some new drinking methods. That's ridiculous. The proper way to drink alcohol is to pour it into a glass, bring the glass to your mouth, and swallow. Anything beyond that is just making things complicated.

jokes.text: This is the wrong way to consume alcohol.
jokes.setup: Ron just said 'there's no wrong way to consume alcohol' about 12 seconds ago
jokes.punchline: Seeing the molecular cocktail experience, Ron immediately abandons his principle
jokes.explanation: A nearly perfect callback. The setup (Joke 20) has barely left the audience's memory when this lands, and the exact verbatim inversion — 'there IS a wrong way to consume alcohol' — is as tight a callback structure as television comedy produces. Ron's philosophical certainty is demolished in under a minute by a fog cloud cocktail. The economy is flawless — the joke is eight words. This is among the best jokes in the episode and is exceptional by any measure. Approaches the 9.5 anchor in structural craft, though not quite as culturally resonant.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I'll just have a regular beer, please.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Coming right up.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Here's your beer.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: What is this? It looks like a science experiment.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: It's a beer sphere. The flavor bursts on your tongue.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I just wanted a normal beer in a normal glass.

jokes.text: Visual: Ron staring at a stiff alcohol cloud/foam where his drink should be — 'Whoa, that's a pretty stiff cloud.'
jokes.setup: The molecular martini has been chiseled — it appears to be a solid cloud of foam
jokes.punchline: Ron's reaction — applying his normal 'strong drink' appreciation ('stiff') to a cloud of foam — shows he's trying to process this within his normal framework
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag. Ron applying his whiskey-drinker's vocabulary to a cloud of molecular foam ('stiff cloud') is a funny culture-clash moment. Works better with the visual of Ron looking at what is essentially a cocktail-flavored cumulus.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: There is no wrong way to drink.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Well, there is one wrong way.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Out of a bowl.

jokes.text: It's a whiskey-infused lotion. / Can I ask if this entire establishment is a practical joke of some kind?
jokes.setup: Ron orders Scotch; the bartender produces a lotion and begins applying it to Ron's hands
jokes.punchline: Ron's measured, almost forensic inquiry as to whether the bar is 'a practical joke' — delivered with Swansonian gravity rather than outrage
jokes.explanation: Ron's response to whiskey lotion is perfectly calibrated — not an outburst, not slapstick, but a sincere philosophical inquiry. The phrase 'practical joke of some kind' is wonderfully formal for someone having lotion applied to their hands. Strong character integration — only Ron would frame this as a calm investigative question rather than a complaint.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: It's served as lotion you rub on your hands

jokes.text: If you don't like the Scotch, they have a vodka that's served in the form of a flash of light.
jokes.setup: Ron has just questioned the whiskey lotion; Tom offers the alternative
jokes.punchline: A vodka served as a literal flash of light — escalating the absurdism from 'fog cloud' to 'topical lotion' to 'flash of light,' each less drinkable than the last
jokes.explanation: The escalation from cloud to lotion to flash of light is a well-constructed absurdist run. Each step moves further from actual drinking while maintaining bar vocabulary. 'A flash of light' as a cocktail delivery mechanism is genuinely inspired — it's the logical endpoint of the bar's conceit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Wait, they brought you a drink? And then another drink? Without you asking? And it kept happening?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: This has to be a prank. Someone's pranking us.

jokes.text: Well, four years of work down the drain, and I have a penis on my head.
jokes.setup: Leslie is devastated about Jamm's development site coup and is sad-drinking at what appears to be a bachelorette party bar
jokes.punchline: The visual incongruity of Leslie delivering an anguished career lament while wearing a penis hat — the hat is implied by bachelorette party context established earlier
jokes.explanation: This line is a great synthesis of the episode's two tones — Leslie's earnest professional despair and the bachelorette party absurdity. 'And I have a penis on my head' as an addendum to a serious lament is perfectly structured. The casual self-awareness of acknowledging the hat while in genuine distress is peak Leslie Knope — she can hold both realities simultaneously. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: We have alternatives to lotion Scotch. We can inject it directly into your eyeballs.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Or we can just pour it into your ear canal and let it drip down into your brain.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Or, if you're feeling adventurous, we can turn it into a suppository.

jokes.text: My dream is dead, Ann. Mine too. This is why I prefer nightmares.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are having a sincere moment of despair about the park project
jokes.punchline: April interjects with 'This is why I prefer nightmares' — a completely sincere, deeply dark personal philosophy delivered as natural conversational participation
jokes.explanation: April at her very best. 'This is why I prefer nightmares' is a line that works on multiple levels: it's dark, it's absurdly logical within April's worldview (you can't be disappointed by outcomes you already expected to be terrible), and it's delivered as genuine comfort-advice. Only April Ludgate could say this. Extremely quotable. Among the best April lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm wearing penis-themed party gear because I'm embracing my sexuality and supporting my friend's last night of freedom!

jokes.text: You are sad drinking right now, and I need you to be happy drinking. Like when we watch Grease together.
jokes.setup: Leslie is clearly wallowing; Ann tries to redirect her
jokes.punchline: The specific reference to 'watching Grease together' as a specific context for 'happy drinking' — an oddly specific and endearing detail about their friendship
jokes.explanation: The distinction between 'sad drinking' and 'happy drinking' is a solid comedic concept, and the Grease specification adds a sweet, character-grounding detail. Not a huge laugh but contributes to the warm character texture that Parks does well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: My dream is dead.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I prefer nightmares. At least when you wake up from those, you're relieved.

jokes.text: Yet another piece of Wamapoke land plowed over by the white man.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been talking about losing the park land to development; Ken is sitting nearby
jokes.punchline: Ken's perfectly timed interjection — joining Leslie's lament with his own historical grievance, delivered with the same matter-of-fact tone as his earlier jokes
jokes.explanation: Ken's comedic voice is at its most effective here — the interjection pivots a private moment into a statement that recontextualizes the whole episode's stakes. The line is darkly funny because it's completely true and Ken says it with the same casual weariness as everything else. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. I just planted that artifact in the ground so we could excavate it and make the park look historically significant. That's... that's illegal, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh my God. I'm a criminal. I'm going to jail. I'm going to be somebody's prison wife.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm Jennifer Barkley's prison wife. Nobody else's.

jokes.text: Oh, this is bad. I should not have done this.
jokes.setup: Leslie has apparently buried Wamapoke artifacts on the development site to stop construction — and is now realizing the implications
jokes.punchline: The talking-head reaction after the fact — Leslie's simple, direct acknowledgment of her own mistake with no spin or justification, delivered in a small voice
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the confession's simplicity — Leslie's elaborate scheme, reduced to a two-sentence self-assessment with no rhetorical hedging. It's a nice Leslie moment but the joke is fairly light.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that an Abraham Lincoln stripper?

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Yeah, I booked him. I call him 'Honest Babe.'

jokes.text: Well, if it isn't Babe Lincoln! Hello, ladies. I'm Abraham Lincoln. Who's the lucky Mary Todd?
jokes.setup: Ann has organized an Abraham Lincoln stripper for Leslie's bachelorette party
jokes.punchline: The stripper introduces himself with his stage persona ('Babe Lincoln'), the visual of a Lincoln-costumed stripper, and the question 'who's the lucky Mary Todd?' treating Lincoln's assassination-widowed wife as a romantic prize
jokes.explanation: The 'Babe Lincoln' name is excellent — it's exactly the kind of pun a stripper service would use, and it's perfectly calibrated to Leslie's well-known love of female historical figures and the American presidency. The Mary Todd framing is a nice secondary gag. Strong setup for the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: I'm about to issue my own Emancipation Proclamation... of these abs!

jokes.text: Abraham Lincoln male stripper arrives at the bachelorette party
jokes.setup: The bachelorette party is in a funk due to the Paunch Burger situation
jokes.punchline: A male stripper dressed as Abraham Lincoln arrives — 'Well, if it isn't Babe Lincoln!'
jokes.explanation: The Abraham Lincoln stripper is a good absurdist choice — the show has always given Leslie a reverence for Lincoln, making an objectified Lincoln particularly funny. 'Babe Lincoln' is a decent pun. The concept is stronger than the execution of the individual lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Come on, live a little. You've definitely had Lincoln sex dreams.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? No! Why would I... I mean, sure, he's tall and powerful, but...

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Leslie, you literally have a portrait of Lincoln in your office.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, I'm just not in the mood for historical nudity. Please, Mr. president, put your pants back on.
jokes.setup: The Lincoln stripper is performing; Leslie is too distracted by the Jamm situation to participate
jokes.punchline: 'Historical nudity' as a category — and the formal address 'Mr. president' to the stripper — Leslie's inability to disengage her professional respectfulness even while rejecting a strip show
jokes.explanation: Leslie cannot stop being Leslie even in front of a stripper. 'Historical nudity' is an invented category that is exactly how Leslie would characterize a Lincoln strip show — she's created a taxonomy. 'Mr. president, put your pants back on' is Leslie respecting the office of the presidency even while dismissing the performer. Deeply character-specific and highly quotable. Strong craft.

dialogue.speaker: Glenn
dialogue.line: Four score and seven years ago, our fathers brought forth on this continent a new nation, conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal. Now that nation is about to see me naked.

jokes.text: Is your name Glenn? / Yeah. / I sat behind you in middle school band. Do you still play the clarinet?
jokes.setup: Ann is standing awkwardly near the Lincoln stripper after Leslie has rejected the performance
jokes.punchline: Ann recognizes the stripper as a former classmate and immediately pivots to chitchat about middle school band — the most mundane possible response to encountering a stripper
jokes.explanation: A beautifully awkward moment. The comedy is in Ann's social instinct to be friendly and normal overriding the inherent weirdness of the situation. Asking a half-naked Lincoln if he still plays the clarinet is exactly the kind of cringe-worthy but sweet interaction Ann would have. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Oh my god, it's you! You were at the club last night!

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was working.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I know. I was there too. We should hang out sometime.

jokes.text: Man, if I ever have a bachelor party, I am definitely coming back here. / You never had one before you were married to Wendy? / No, it was a green card wedding. I did watch the three-way sex scene from Wild Things a few times the night before, but it didn't really count.
jokes.setup: The group is enjoying Essence bar and the topic of bachelor parties comes up
jokes.punchline: Tom's casual disclosure that his marriage was a green card wedding and that his pre-wedding celebration was watching a specific sex scene from a 1998 thriller 'a few times' — delivered with total normalcy
jokes.explanation: The Wild Things sex scene was a genuinely famous piece of 90s pop culture, which makes this very specific — Tom didn't watch a movie, he watched ONE scene specifically, multiple times, alone, the night before his green card wedding. The specificity is what makes this joke land. It's also a perfectly Tom Haverford thing to do.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I never had a bachelor party because it wasn't a real marriage. Wendy needed citizenship.

jokes.text: Me and April, we got married with no warning. I didn't even have time to take a shower before my wedding. / Or after. / For, like, a week and a half.
jokes.setup: Andy explains he didn't have a bachelor party because his wedding was spontaneous
jokes.punchline: April confirms he didn't shower after either — and Andy specifies 'for like a week and a half' — the escalation from 'no shower before' to 'no shower for ten days post-wedding' is the joke
jokes.explanation: A great two-beat escalation. The callback structure is clean: April confirms the 'or after' to add the second beat, then Andy's specific '...a week and a half' clarification lands the punchline. April's laconic 'Or after' is perfect — she's not horrified, just noting a fact. Deeply in character for both Andy and April.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Didn't shower for over a week including the wedding

jokes.text: Tammy One forbade me from any kind of celebration, and Tammy Two thwarted me by calling in a bomb threat to the steakhouse.
jokes.setup: Ron explains he also never had a bachelor party — the reasons are each associated with one of his ex-wives
jokes.punchline: Tammy Two's specific and extreme response (calling in a bomb threat) to Ron's bachelor party plans — the escalation from 'forbade' (control) to 'bomb threat' (terrorism) in a casual sentence
jokes.explanation: The contrast between the two Tammys is perfectly calibrated: Tammy One forbade (controlling, authoritarian), Tammy Two called in a bomb threat (chaotic, unhinged). Both outcomes are extreme in different directions. The casual delivery — 'thwarted me by calling in a bomb threat' — treats terrorism as a minor inconvenience, which is exactly the right register for Tammy Two comedy. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I never had a bachelor party. Tammy Two wouldn't allow it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: She said if I went to one, she'd key my car, burn my house down, and poison my dog.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I believed her.

jokes.text: I didn't have one either! / Yeah, really, it's a funny story. So two weeks before I married Gayle, I had an emergency appendectomy. / Boop! That's me hitting the snooze button. Don't talk again for another ten minutes.
jokes.setup: Everyone in the group has shared their lack-of-bachelor-party story; Jerry eagerly jumps in to participate
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'Boop! That's me hitting the snooze button. Don't talk again for another ten minutes.' — the group reflexively shuts Jerry down mid-story, so accustomed to dismissing him that Ben creates a specific metaphor for it
jokes.explanation: The Jerry gag is a Parks running gag that varies in quality, but this execution is excellent. Ben's 'snooze button' metaphor is creative — it implies Jerry's voice is literally just an alarm to be silenced, and 'Don't talk again for another ten minutes' sets an arbitrary precise timer on his existence. The 'Boop!' sound effect is the perfect physical gesture completion.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: So at my bachelor party, we went to this club and—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, Jerry, Jerry. Stop. I don't have time for your stories. Actually, you know what? I'm gonna use you as my alarm clock.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wake me up at 6 AM tomorrow morning by doing that thing where you say something that makes no sense.

jokes.text: Welcome to Tom's bachelor party, held in a white airplane hangar from the ice planet Hoth, replete with dangling, beautiful aerialists.
jokes.setup: Tom declares everyone will get the bachelor party they never had, and his own vision is announced first
jokes.punchline: Tom's bachelor party is a Star Wars reference combined with a Cirque du Soleil setup — the specific detail of 'ice planet Hoth' combined with 'aerialists' is uniquely Tom Haverford maximalism
jokes.explanation: The Hoth detail is a bit odd for Tom's character (typically more hip-hop/fashion/luxury than Star Wars) but 'white airplane hangar' as a visual reference to Hoth is fun, and 'replete with dangling, beautiful aerialists' is exactly Tom's voice. Character-consistent with Tom's grandiosity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: To my beautiful bride, Beyoncé. I know we've only known each other for three minutes, but I feel like this is going to work out.

jokes.text: Hey, hey-- and to my bride, Rihanna. We truly did find love in a hopeless place.
jokes.setup: Tom is toasting at his imaginary bachelor party
jokes.punchline: Tom's imaginary bride is Rihanna — and he quotes her own song lyric ('We Found Love in a Hopeless Place') as if it's a meaningful personal sentiment, not a pop song
jokes.explanation: Tom's celebrity crush on Rihanna is established enough as a character beat that this lands well. Using Rihanna's own lyric as a wedding toast to her is a nice self-referential touch that works for Tom's character. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I think the real issue is—

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Okay, we don't need your input right now.

jokes.text: Well, I buried a bunch of Wamapoke artifacts in the dirt so that people would find them and have to stop developing at the site. You know, when I say it out loud, it doesn't sound so bad. / No, that's bad. / Yeah, that's pretty uncool.
jokes.setup: Leslie confesses her scheme; she's trying to frame it positively
jokes.punchline: Leslie's delusional 'it doesn't sound so bad' is immediately punctured by Ann and April's simultaneous corrections — but the real joke is Leslie's self-delusion in the first place
jokes.explanation: Leslie's capacity for motivated reasoning about her own ethical lapses is a consistent character trait. The beat where she talks herself into thinking it's fine, only to be instantly corrected by her friends, is well-executed. 'Shut up, Glenn' as an aside is a nice extra touch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Come on, everyone! These penis party favors are perfect for digging. Just use them like real shovels!

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Leslie, they're not actually functional tools.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude, Ben. Now dig!

jokes.text: I tried to sneaky him back, and it turned to crummy, and I have to undo it.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining the logic chain of her ethical lapse
jokes.punchline: 'Sneaky him back' and 'turned to crummy' — Leslie's invented verb constructions reduce moral reasoning to child-level vocabulary, which is funnier for how seriously she takes it
jokes.explanation: Leslie's made-up word constructions are a comedic hallmark. 'Sneaky him back' as a verb is particularly good — it treats sneakiness as a transitive action you can perform on someone. The moral logic ('he sneakied, so I sneakied back, and then crummy happened') is childlike in its structure but delivered with Leslie's characteristic seriousness.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: She's got beautiful blonde hair, perfect skin, amazing legs... but she's not really my type.

jokes.text: You guys, the penis hats cut your digging time in half. I'm serious. Don't be afraid. Use the penises.
jokes.setup: Leslie, Ann, and April are in the dark digging up the buried artifacts; they are apparently using their bachelorette party accessories as tools
jokes.punchline: The practical application of novelty penis hats as digging implements — Leslie's no-nonsense 'Use the penises' instruction delivered with the same energy as any work directive
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The callback to the bachelorette party's penis theme pays off completely unexpectedly — the items that were going to be fun party props are now field tools for a covert archaeological operation. 'Use the penises' as a direct command is extraordinarily funny in its total commitment to pragmatism. Leslie has no time for irony; she has holes to dig. The specificity ('cut your digging time in half') treating the penis hats as legitimate equipment is inspired. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: How did Jerry get Gayle? I mean, look at him. He's a disaster. Did he save her life? Does she owe him money? Is she in witness protection and he's her handler? Did they get drunk in Vegas? Is she being blackmailed? Did he win her in a poker game? Is she a robot? Did she lose a bet? Is she his prisoner?

jokes.text: Perkins does it again.
jokes.setup: Leslie and April are apparently in the middle of digging when Leslie pauses to give a confessional evaluation
jokes.punchline: Leslie credits Ann — who organized the bachelorette party that inadvertently provided the penis hat tools — with the success of the digging operation, as though Ann had planned this all along
jokes.explanation: A quick button on Joke 43. The attribution of digging efficiency to Ann's planning is absurd and sweet — Leslie's loyalty to Ann makes her give Ann credit even for an accidental solution. The 'whoo' that follows caps it as a confessional celebration.

dialogue.speaker: Sherm
dialogue.line: That's too bad, Gary.

jokes.text: She was slender. Blonde hair, big breasts, long legs. Ugh, not my type at all. / And what was it, exactly, that led to you two hitting it off? Was she ill, or did your father witness her father committing a crime? Or was she temporarily blind--
jokes.setup: Jerry describes his wife Gayle in glowing physical terms at the steakhouse; the group is confused about how Jerry landed someone so apparently beautiful
jokes.punchline: Ron's rapid-fire list of hypothetical disasters that would explain why an attractive woman would marry Jerry — 'Was she ill? Did your father witness her father committing a crime? Was she temporarily blind?' — each more extreme and creative than the last
jokes.explanation: Ron's list of Jerry-wife hypotheticals is genuinely inspired. The escalation goes from medical ('ill') to blackmail ('father witnessed a crime') to sensory impairment ('temporarily blind') — each explanation more baroque than the last. Ron is trying, with utmost sincerity, to find a logical explanation for Gayle's existence, because it violates the natural order. This is deeply Ron AND deeply Jerry simultaneously. Among the best-crafted jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Sherm
dialogue.line: I'm always ready. Jerry drops his ice cream cone at least twice a week. I keep a spare in my pocket at all times.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Was she ill, or did your father witness her father committing a crime? Or was she temporarily blind--'
jokes.setup: The guys are asking what drew Jerry and Gayle together, since Ron says she was so conventionally attractive she wasn't Ron's type
jokes.punchline: Andy's list of reasons a beautiful woman would marry Jerry — all of them terrible — reveals Andy's (and everyone's) genuine surprise at the match
jokes.explanation: Andy's escalating list of reasons Gayle would marry Jerry is sweetly cruel — they're all scenarios where she had no choice. 'Temporarily blind' is the best item on the list. The fact that he's genuinely trying to understand rather than being purely mean is Andy-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: My ideal bachelor party would start with a pickup basketball game with Michael Jordan, then we'd go to a strip club where Dave Matthews is the DJ, then we'd somehow make Tom Brady cry, and then I'd hook up with Dave Matthews.

jokes.text: I always make a backup cone. He drops it about half the time.
jokes.setup: Jerry has dropped his ice cream cone (presumably) while being toasted; the shop owner produces a replacement immediately
jokes.punchline: The owner's backstory that Jerry drops it approximately 50% of the time — confirming Jerry's haplessness is so reliable that service industry workers have adapted their operations around it
jokes.explanation: An excellent background joke that earns its place. The shop owner has a backup cone prepared because Jerry's incompetence is so predictable that it's been absorbed into store policy. 'About half the time' is the precise qualifier that makes it perfect — not 'always,' which would be absurd, but 'half the time,' which is exactly pathetic enough. One of the better Jerry jokes in the series because it's observational rather than mean-spirited.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Is this heaven? Did I die? Oh my God, I died! I'm in heaven!

jokes.text: Well, mine's impossible. I want to see a Colts game. I want to see the Colts beat the Patriots 49 to nothing, then I yell at Tom Brady and make him cry, then I hook up with Dave Matthews, and we play golden tee for ten hours.
jokes.setup: Tom asks each bachelor what activity they'd choose for their perfect party; Andy is told to name anything
jokes.punchline: Andy's scenario begins reasonably (Colts game) but immediately escalates: making Tom Brady cry, hooking up with Dave Matthews (the musician), and ten hours of Golden Tee (an arcade golf game) — the Dave Matthews detail is the absurdist peak
jokes.explanation: This is the most Andy Dwyer sentence ever written. The list starts with a genuine sports fantasy, pivots to bullying Tom Brady (emotional wish fulfillment), then 'hook up with Dave Matthews' (bisexual, casual, oddly specific celebrity choice), then ten hours of a bar arcade game as the denouement. Each element is perfectly Andy — the priorities are chaos, the specificity is random, and the Dave Matthews detail is the kind of choice that reveals a person's complete inner world. Highly quotable and deeply character-integrated. Approaches the 8.0 anchor easily.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Wait, really? You think I could actually play in the NFL?

dialogue.speaker: Jim Irsay
dialogue.line: Well, you've certainly got the size for it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Oh man, this is happening. This is really happening. I'm gonna be a professional football player. I'm gonna buy a huge house, and a Ferrari, and... and I'll finally be able to afford those artisanal popsicles I've been wanting.

jokes.text: I'm dead. I am dead. And this is what heaven is like. I knew it. Oh, this is where they play the games!
jokes.setup: Andy is brought to Lucas Oil Stadium and begins to realize where he is
jokes.punchline: Andy's escalating existential response to the stadium — he immediately concludes he has died and this is the afterlife, and his confirmation ('I knew it') implies he always suspected heaven would be a sports stadium
jokes.explanation: Andy's worldview is so narrow and pure that the stadium triggers a genuine existential reassessment. 'I knew it' as a reaction to discovering heaven is a Colts stadium is deeply Andy — he accepts this without question. 'Oh, this is where they play the games!' as a final line is a perfect child-like epiphany delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I wore a football jersey to my wedding.

jokes.text: I can't look at you, Reggie Wayne. Oh. / I got married in your jersey. That's no joke. / That's weird. But I respect that.
jokes.setup: Andy is meeting NFL players and meeting Reggie Wayne specifically triggers an emotional response
jokes.punchline: Andy's claim to have been married in Reggie Wayne's jersey — and Reggie Wayne's perfectly calibrated response ('That's weird. But I respect that.') — Reggie playing along graciously with the bit
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Andy's genuine, overwhelming emotional response to a football player he loves (consistent with his character), and Reggie Wayne's response — 'That's weird. But I respect that' is exactly the right reaction, balancing honest assessment with sportsmanlike acceptance. The real NFL players playing themselves adds a meta-layer.

dialogue.speaker: Reggie Wayne
dialogue.line: That's a bold choice wearing my jersey to your own wedding. But hey, I respect the hustle.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not mad?

dialogue.speaker: Reggie Wayne
dialogue.line: Mad? Nah man. You're out here representing. Just maybe next time wear it under the tux, you know what I'm saying?

jokes.text: Okay, guy, settle down. / Uh, Mr. Andrew Luck, it's every groom's dream to catch a touchdown pass thrown by you. Could you do me the honor? / Yeah, let's do it. / Keep the spiral tight. / I'll try.
jokes.setup: Chris is facilitating Andy's football fantasy with extreme formality
jokes.punchline: Chris addresses the NFL quarterback as 'Mr. Andrew Luck' with the gravity of a formal diplomatic request — and Luck's 'I'll try' in response to 'keep the spiral tight' is a beautifully understated joke about an NFL quarterback promising to 'try' at his primary skill
jokes.explanation: Chris's formality as a comedic register is well-deployed here. 'Mr. Andrew Luck' is a funny honorific for the circumstances. The 'I'll try' from Andrew Luck is a self-deprecating joke from a professional quarterback that works because it's understated and unexpected.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: And then Donna showed up in a helicopter, and she was like, 'Everyone get in the helicopter!' And we all flew to this private island where we had dinner with Oprah and The Rock.

jokes.text: Chris talking head about Jim Irsay: 'Jim gave them Colts tickets and autographed jerseys. They preferred Jim.'
jokes.setup: Chris explains his friendship with Jim Irsay through a shared charity mentoring program
jokes.punchline: 'They preferred Jim' — Chris's flat acknowledgment that a state house tour loses to Colts tickets and jerseys, delivered without complaint
jokes.explanation: The three-word punchline 'They preferred Jim' is a masterpiece of economy. The setup is perfect — Chris genuinely proud of his tours — and the landing is completely deflating and completely understandable. Chris's sunny acceptance of this verdict is very in character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, so the Lincoln impersonator we hired for the party is now doing manual labor with us?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Yeah, he needed the work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So the Lincoln stripper is now doing manual labor.

jokes.text: We're having the time of our lives, and I'm calling you to rub it in! / ...We went to an insane bar, played football with the Colts. / Football! / Now we're going to a steakhouse. What are you doing? / Uh, well, we're surrounded by hot guys.
jokes.setup: Leslie calls Ann to brag about the bachelor party; Ann is in fact digging up artifacts with penis hats
jokes.punchline: Ann's lie — 'we're surrounded by hot guys' — while she's actually doing covert archaeological work in a parking lot with a bachelorette party accessory. The dramatic irony is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the dramatic irony — we know Ann is lying because we've seen what she's actually doing. Leslie's triumphant call (football with the Colts!) contrasted with Ann's beleaguered reality (underground artifact recovery) is a nice parallel structure for the episode's A/B plots.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Wait, did you say Gingrich? As in... Newt Gingrich?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: That's my last name. Well, not exactly, but... Do you think we might be related?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: I mean, it's possible. My family tree isn't exactly... well documented.

jokes.text: Oh, Donna just ripped off a stripper's underwear with her teeth. / Whoo!
jokes.setup: Ann is fabricating bachelorette party fun while actually digging holes
jokes.punchline: Ann's improvised lie specifically features Donna's signature behavior — it's plausible enough that it might even be true (given Donna's established character), and Donna's 'Whoo!' confirms it without confirming anything
jokes.explanation: The Donna detail works because it's so plausible for Donna — the lie is nearly indistinguishable from reality. Donna's reflexive 'Whoo!' of affirmation (while presumably digging) is a nice character beat. Solid comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I went to a molecular mixology bar last week. The bartender asked me what I wanted to drink. I said 'whiskey.' He said 'what form?' I said 'liquid.' Apparently that was wrong.

jokes.text: Ann, who are you lying to? / Shh. / No! / Can I take a break? My hands are tired. / Uh-uh. We paid for an hour.
jokes.setup: Ann is on the phone lying to the bachelor party group; April, who is digging alongside, calls her out; the stripper Glenn is also apparently helping dig
jokes.punchline: Glenn the stripper asking for a break and Ann treating him like a contracted labor resource — 'We paid for an hour' — the stripper has been deployed as a digging laborer
jokes.explanation: The full payoff of the 'Glenn from middle school band' joke. Having recruited her old acquaintance (who happens to be a stripper she's already paid for an hour) as manual labor is a genuinely original comedic development. 'We paid for an hour' treating the stripper like a hired contractor is a great subversion. The callback makes this funnier than it would be standalone.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have strong feelings for Diane. She's smart, she's talented, she's beautiful, and she makes me want to be a better man.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, that's... that's really sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Did Ron just say feelings? Out loud?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I think hell just froze over.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron Swanson said the word 'beautiful' about a woman. This is historic.

jokes.text: Tonight we eat something's flesh! / I want meat!
jokes.setup: The group arrives at St. Elmo's Steak House
jokes.punchline: Ron's primal framing of steak dinner as a meat-eating ritual ('something's flesh') followed immediately by Andy's caveman endorsement
jokes.explanation: 'Tonight we eat something's flesh' is a great Ron line — carnivore enthusiasm elevated to tribal declaration. The Andy echo ('I want meat!') reduces it further to pure instinct. Both lines are perfectly on-brand for each character.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I would describe my feelings for Diane as... adequate.

jokes.text: Jerry, are you sure this is our table? There's only four settings. / Excuse me, sir. This is not your table. Well, I thought you said the Gergich party. / No, no, I said the Gingrich party. / Oh, my gosh, I'm so sorry. Damn it, Jerry. / But you know what? Gingrich, Gergich. I wonder if we're related. / I don't think so, Jerry.
jokes.setup: The bachelor party group arrives at the steakhouse; there seems to be a table issue
jokes.punchline: Jerry has led them to the wrong table — specifically Newt Gingrich's table — and Jerry's genuine wonderment about whether he and Newt Gingrich might be related because their names rhyme
jokes.explanation: A great Jerry joke. The Gingrich/Gergich confusion is so perfect it's almost too perfect — the names are identical in every way except one phoneme. Jerry's earnest 'I wonder if we're related' based purely on the name similarity is the right level of Jerry naivety. 'I don't think so, Jerry' is a perfect deadpan button.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Prison is actually pretty great. You get three meals a day, a bed, and nobody bothers you. It's like a spa, but with bars and murder.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: April, that's not helping.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Plus, you don't have to worry about rent or your job. It's basically early retirement.

jokes.text: I'd like four more glasses of Lagavulin in liquid form. / That's not something you really need to specify. / You'd be surprised.
jokes.setup: Ron orders whisky at the steakhouse; the waiter notes that Lagavulin is by definition liquid
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'You'd be surprised' — a direct callback to the molecular mixology bar, indicating Ron has been so traumatized by non-liquid alcohol delivery that he now specifies 'liquid form' as a precaution
jokes.explanation: This callback is exceptional. 'I'd like four more glasses of Lagavulin in liquid form' as a specific request earns an eyebrow raise from the waiter — 'that's not something you really need to specify.' Ron's 'You'd be surprised' is the perfect three-word callback that tells the entire story of the molecular bar in a single phrase. It rewards the audience for watching, it's deeply in character for Ron, and 'You'd be surprised' as a line has the right amount of weight and resignation. This is among the three best jokes in the episode. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Construction worker
dialogue.line: We haven't found any dinosaur bones, no ancient artifacts, no religious relics...

dialogue.speaker: Construction worker
dialogue.line: Basically nothing from any of the weird countries.

jokes.text: So, bachelor boy, how's it going with Diane? Hmm. / I'm gonna be very candid with you all. I like her. / Whoa! / Wow!
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ron about Diane; Ron takes a beat to consider
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'I like her' — delivered as a profound confession of deep romantic vulnerability, and received by the group as a shocking revelation — the disconnect between Ron's extreme emotional reticence and the ordinariness of the statement
jokes.explanation: For Ron Swanson, 'I like her' is the emotional equivalent of a Shakespearean love sonnet. The group's stunned reactions ('Whoa!' 'Wow!') perfectly mirror the audience's understanding that this is Ron at maximum emotional openness. The joke is entirely in the gap between the ordinariness of the phrase and its enormous significance coming from this specific character. Excellent character integration — this joke doesn't work with anyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Construction Worker
dialogue.line: Hey, we found something weird buried out here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Construction Worker
dialogue.line: A bunch of gummy penises. They're still in the package.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Those are from Leslie's bachelorette party!

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: How deep were they buried?

dialogue.speaker: Construction Worker
dialogue.line: About three feet down.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Leslie really committed to that party.

jokes.text: There are so many things that I could say about Ron, but I think that the best man's speech should represent the groom. So I will just say... / To Ron.
jokes.setup: Chris is giving a bachelor party toast for Ron; he builds up to saying something meaningful
jokes.punchline: After the elaborate setup of representing the groom, Chris's entire toast is just 'To Ron' — but Ben's response ('Just perfect. Perfect, Chris.') treats this as genuinely artful
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Chris's elaborate setup promises depth, but 'To Ron' is the only toast Ron would actually want — maximum sincerity, minimum words, no sentimentality. Ben's 'Just perfect. Perfect, Chris' affirms that Chris has understood Ron completely. It's a joke about reading the room correctly. The economy is excellent — 'To Ron' is two words that say everything.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: April, you are so smart, and capable, and funny, and beautiful, and fertile.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Did you just compliment my ability to reproduce?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I did. You're welcome.

jokes.text: Your meal has already been taken care of by Mr. Hibbert. / What's up, Jell-o shot? / I am not paying for that guy. He owes me a lot of money.
jokes.setup: The group is surprised when their meal is paid for; Roy Hibbert (NBA player, Entertainment 720 connection) appears
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate pivot to 'I am not paying for that guy. He owes me a lot of money.' — the return of the Entertainment 720 bankruptcy storyline as a cameo gag
jokes.explanation: Roy Hibbert's 'What's up, Jell-o shot?' is a fun character-specific greeting for Tom (referencing their Entertainment 720 days). Tom's deadpan 'He owes me a lot of money' as a response to a friendly celebrity paying for dinner is a good dark comic beat. Rewards fans familiar with the E720 arc.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I know what you mean. Leslie's compliments can be a lot sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're not friends, Ann. We will never be friends. I don't even like you.

jokes.text: Yes, please. Take extra cream, 30 sugars.
jokes.setup: A waiter offers coffee; Jerry accepts with particular specifications
jokes.punchline: '30 sugars' — an absurd quantity that is simultaneously a character joke (Jerry's general excess and haplessness) and an absurdist non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: A background character joke — 30 sugars is funny because it's so precisely specific and so vastly unreasonable. Jerry's inability to function normally extends to coffee orders. Doesn't do heavy lifting but is a nice texture joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: It was illegal to smell like a Native American.

jokes.text: I can't believe I tried to exploit the Wamapoke for my own personal gain. / Well, we got most of the artifacts, and even if we didn't, they probably won't find them. / Yeah, and if they do, you'll just go to jail. But you can make wine in your toilet and fight people, which is a super-cool way to live.
jokes.setup: Leslie is feeling guilty about the artifact burial scheme; Ann and April offer reassurance
jokes.punchline: April's consolation is that jail has its own upside — toilet wine and fighting — delivered with complete sincerity as though this is a reasonable perspective
jokes.explanation: April's jail pitch — toilet wine and fighting as selling points — is delivered as genuine comfort advice. 'Super-cool way to live' as a sincere assessment is peak April. The dark optimism here is exactly April's brand of encouragement.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: The Holocaust. Slavery. The way we treat our oceans. And... I accidentally threw away the city's only copy of the original town charter.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Oh, my God. Tweep. I tweeped. I called Tweep.' (realizing she can call a reporter)
jokes.setup: Leslie needs help figuring out the Jamm situation
jokes.punchline: 'I tweeped' — Leslie using 'Tweep' (Shauna Malwae-Tweep's name) as a verb meaning 'to call Tweep,' delivered with genuine discovery excitement
jokes.explanation: The verbification of 'Tweep' is a small but effective Leslie Knope word-invention moment. Her genuine excitement at her own realization ('I tweeped!') is endearing. Not a huge laugh but a characteristic Leslie moment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I have to admit something. I didn't actually vote for you for Best Non-Married Guy. I voted for Ryan Gosling.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. Tweep. I tweeped. I called Tweep.
jokes.setup: Leslie realizes she has accidentally called reporter Shauna Malwae-Tweep while panicking about the artifact situation
jokes.punchline: Leslie's self-narration of her own mistake — 'I tweeped' — invented as a verb for accidentally dialing a reporter, delivered with the dawning horror of someone watching a disaster unfold in slow motion
jokes.explanation: Leslie coining 'tweeped' as a verb for accidentally calling Shauna Malwae-Tweep is a lovely character-specific language invention. The triple repetition — 'Tweep. I tweeped. I called Tweep.' — with mounting horror is well-structured. It's a moment that captures Leslie's particular relationship with verbal invention under stress.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: She's gonna be a real smart, beautiful woman. She'll probably be a doctor or a lawyer. They'll have two kids together. A boy and a girl. They'll be happy. But then one day, Tom Haverford will die in a skydiving accident. A mid-air explosion. It'll be tragic.

jokes.text: Look, I'm telling the truth here, lady. We haven't found any American Indian artifacts. Or regular Indian. Japanese, Muslim, Jewish, none of those weird countries.
jokes.setup: A reporter (Shauna) is asking about artifact findings at the construction site; Jamm addresses the camera
jokes.punchline: Jamm's expanding list of ethnicities/religions he hasn't found artifacts from — listing 'Japanese, Muslim, Jewish' as equivalent categories, then calling them 'weird countries' — a perfect portrait of confident ignorance
jokes.explanation: Jamm's taxonomy here — mixing nationalities, religions, and ethnicities into one undifferentiated list of 'weird countries' — is a pitch-perfect satire of a certain kind of confident ignorance. The escalation from 'regular Indian' (as a category opposite to 'American Indian') to 'Muslim' and 'Jewish' as countries is exactly what makes Jamm work as a character. Dark, subversive, character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I'm living like a revenge movie character. I wake up at 5 AM, I do 200 push-ups, I drink a protein shake made of eggs and more eggs, I look at a picture of Chris and April together and I say 'Not today, buddy. Not today.' Then I go to work and I'm better at my job than I've ever been.

jokes.text: Worker finds the artifacts Leslie buried: 'I also found some weird-looking gummy candy.'
jokes.setup: Workers are digging and finding artifacts
jokes.punchline: The 'gummy candy' is clearly the gummy penises from the bachelorette party — Leslie grabbed whatever she had available to bury as 'artifacts'
jokes.explanation: Excellent multi-callback payoff. The gummy penises from the bachelorette party have made it into the Wamapoke artifact excavation site. This is the third callback to penis-shaped items in the episode, each more absurd than the last (eating → digging tool → sacred artifact). The worker's neutral description of 'weird-looking gummy candy' not knowing what it is adds to the absurdity. Well-constructed comedic escalation across the episode.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Ken's like a sad magician who only knows how to make your will to live disappear.

jokes.text: The zodiac killer never confessed. Why do I have to?
jokes.setup: April tells Leslie she needs to come clean to Ken Hotate; Leslie is resistant
jokes.punchline: Leslie's moral framework for confession draws on the Zodiac Killer as a precedent — an absurd parallel that she deploys with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: An exceptional Leslie joke. The logic is impeccably structured: she's looking for precedents that support non-confession, and arrives at the Zodiac Killer — a murderer — as her model. The absurdity of the comparison is the joke, but what makes it truly funny is that Leslie delivers it as a genuine legal/ethical argument. Only Leslie Knope would cite serial killer precedent in a moral dilemma about buried pottery shards. Highly quotable, deeply original.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Was that a threat?

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: You have turned into a very beautiful, wise, and fertile government employee. / Stop. / It's kind of weird when she just starts raining compliments on you, huh? / Don't try to bond with me. / Can't win.
jokes.setup: Leslie sincerely compliments April; the compliments escalate unexpectedly
jokes.punchline: 'Fertile' as one of three sincere compliments Leslie gives April — and then April's rejection of Leslie's attempt to bond over shared discomfort with the compliments
jokes.explanation: 'Fertile' as a sincere Leslie compliment is perfectly unexpected — it fits Leslie's worldview (fertility as a positive attribute) but is bizarre in context. April's 'Don't try to bond with me' / 'Can't win' exchange reveals April has a consistent policy of rejecting Leslie's warmth, which is itself a running gag about April's armor.

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: I offer you this ceremonial peace pipe.

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: Just kidding, it's a regular pipe. I'm going to smoke weed out of it.

jokes.text: Usually you can only get board game t-shirts in XXL.
jokes.setup: Tom has had bachelor party T-shirts made; Ben examines his
jokes.punchline: Ben's immediately specific board game T-shirt sizing observation — revealing a personal history of board game merchandise acquisition that is entirely in character
jokes.explanation: Ten words that reveal Ben has a history of trying to purchase board game T-shirts and being frustrated by the sizing options. It's a background detail of Ben's nerd life delivered completely naturally, as if this is a known consumer problem. The economy is exceptional — maximum character information per word.

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: You? You're going to tell me what's offensive to Native Americans? You're a white man named Jeremy Jamm. Your entire existence is offensive.

jokes.text: We left Jerry back at the gas station in Martinsville. / I'll go get him. / Ah, that guy's the best.
jokes.setup: The group realizes they've lost Jerry during the evening
jokes.punchline: Ben's warm 'Ah, that guy's the best' immediately after remembering Jerry was abandoned at a gas station — the affection and the abandonment coexist without irony
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the simultaneity — 'Ah, that guy's the best' said about someone you just left at a gas station. Ben's genuine fondness is real, and the casualness of both the forgetting and the remembering is very Parks-specific. Gentle running gag execution.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: Hey Chris, do you have a second for lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: Actually, I have approximately 1,200 seconds available during the standard lunch hour, which breaks down to 20 minutes per meal component if we're being efficient. I'm very excited about the nutritional possibilities!

jokes.text: Hey, you know what we should do for him? / Yeah, get him a pet snake, but I keep it.
jokes.setup: Ben suggests they do something nice for Jerry since he missed his bachelor party moment
jokes.punchline: Tom's suggestion — a pet snake that Tom keeps — is framed as Jerry's gift but is actually Tom's acquisition. The benevolence is immediately self-serving.
jokes.explanation: The structure is clean: setup creates expectation of generosity, punchline inverts it completely. 'Get him a pet snake, but I keep it' is economical and perfectly Tom — he can't even fake altruism for a full sentence. The 'but I keep it' reversal is sharp and quick.

jokes.text: In 1951, Pawnee made it illegal for people to, 'Dance or smell like a native American.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to contextualize her own ethical lapse for Ken by establishing how much worse historical Pawnee behavior has been
jokes.punchline: The 1951 law prohibiting people from smelling like a Native American — the legal specificity of 'dance or smell like' as a codified prohibition is the absurdist peak of Pawnee's historical racism
jokes.explanation: The Pawnee history jokes are a consistent vein of the show's satirical world-building. This entry is strong because of the specific absurdity of legislating against smelling like someone — it makes the racism both funnier and more pointed by making it literally sensory. The deadpan delivery of the law as a quote is appropriately horrifying-funny.

jokes.text: I want to raise the bar of awfulness so that when I confess something to you, you have perspective.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been listing atrocities committed against the Wamapoke while Ken listens; she now explains her strategy
jokes.punchline: Leslie explicitly articulating her rhetorical strategy — 'raise the bar of awfulness' to make her confession seem less bad by comparison — is funny because it's transparently self-serving and she doesn't try to hide it
jokes.explanation: Leslie's complete candor about her own manipulation strategy is the joke — she's not hiding the con at all. 'Raise the bar of awfulness' as a phrase is a good Leslie coinage. The self-aware tactical confession is both funny and humanizing.

jokes.text: Andy's interruption: 'I thought you were my friend!' / Chris: 'I thought you were my friend!' (as the villain)
jokes.setup: Chris is in the middle of his elaborate revenge scenario
jokes.punchline: Andy has fully bought into the narrative and is responding in-character with genuine hurt feelings; Chris reciprocates equally in-character
jokes.explanation: Andy getting emotionally invested in the fictional scenario is a good character beat. His genuine hurt and Chris's immediate mirror response shows both characters' earnest natures. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Strange, but sweet. / Only I didn't really die. I was faking it. And I come back. I spy on you from my red Corvette. And I'm planning to kick your ass, but I see how happy you make her, and I have to walk away. I have to. And I do, slowly. In a rainstorm.
jokes.setup: Andy's scenario seemed to end with his generous acceptance of Chris marrying April; Chris labels it 'Strange, but sweet'
jokes.punchline: Andy continues — he wasn't really dead, he faked it, and now he's in a movie-spy revenge subplot complete with red Corvette and slow rainstorm exit — the genre escalation from 'bachelor party toast' to 'action movie
jokes.explanation: Andy's continued elaboration — introducing the fake death, the Corvette, the stakeout, and the slow walk away in rain — is a sustained absurdist escalation. 'And I do, slowly. In a rainstorm.' is the comic peak, delivered with the gravitas of a movie trailer. Andy is narrating his own action film and taking it completely seriously. Good follow-through on Joke 71.

jokes.text: Okay, this isn't really in the spirit of what we're trying to do. / But as time goes by, it eats away at me. You're out living it up with my wife. And I'm alone. In a cave. Training.
jokes.setup: Ben tries to redirect the toast back to Chris; Andy ignores this and continues his revenge narrative
jokes.punchline: Andy is now training in a cave — the scenario has fully transitioned from romance to martial arts revenge film — and 'Training.' as a single-word final sentence is a perfect button
jokes.explanation: The escalation trilogy culminates here. 'In a cave. Training.' is magnificent in its economy — two fragments that complete the Batman/Rocky revenge arc Andy has constructed in a bachelor party toast. Ben's increasingly futile attempts to redirect make the joke better. 'Training.' alone as a sentence is perfectly delivered.

jokes.text: I thought you were my friend. / I thought you were my friend!
jokes.setup: Andy's toast to Chris has become Andy confronting Chris in-character about the fictional future betrayal
jokes.punchline: Andy repeats the accusation at higher intensity — the repetition and the emotional investment in a completely fictional scenario is the joke
jokes.explanation: The button on the whole Andy toast sequence. Andy has so completely inhabited his fictional revenge scenario that he's accusing Chris of a betrayal that hasn't happened and isn't going to happen. The repeated 'I thought you were my friend!' with increasing volume captures Andy's complete loss of narrative/reality distinction.

jokes.text: He really plays white people like a fiddle. Wow. It's amazing to watch.
jokes.setup: Ken Hotate has delivered an eloquent speech shaming Councilman Jamm with historical Wamapoke land grievances
jokes.punchline: Leslie and Ann watch Ken work with pure admiration — 'plays white people like a fiddle' — Leslie's complete self-awareness that she is among the white people being played, and her wholehearted appreciation of it
jokes.explanation: Leslie's admiration for Ken is made funnier by her complete lack of defensiveness — she is absolutely a white person being played, and she respects the craft.
