'Plays white people like a fiddle' is a great phrase that recontextualizes the entire Ken Hotate characterization from the episode's opening. 'It's amazing to watch' as a pure craft appreciation adds a lovely comedic coda.

jokes.text: In the spirit of fair play, I suggest we put on these authentic Wamapoke headdresses and dance around the table. / Absolutely not. / That sounds highly offensive. / Does it, white man? / No. It's not offensive. / So let's do it. / You first. / So clearly, this is not offensive. / It is offensive. / I am very sorry. / Take it off.
jokes.setup: Ken proposes that everyone wear headdresses and dance; the officials resist because it sounds offensive
jokes.punchline: Ken reverses course — it IS offensive, the officials have put on headdresses and are dancing, and Ken watches them embarrass themselves while he sits calmly
jokes.explanation: The perfect final Ken Hotate joke. The structure mirrors Joke 1 (fire water) exactly — a statement that could be sincere or a joke, with white people guessing wrong about which it is. The escalation is magnificent: officials deny it's offensive → Ken says it's not offensive → they put on headdresses → Ken says it IS offensive → they've already made fools of themselves. 'Does it, white man?' is a perfectly chilling pivot line. Ken Hotate is one of the great single-episode characters in Parks history, and this scene is the apex.

jokes.text: A group of good friends having fun, doing nice things for each other. I mean, that's what's important in life, and I want to write about it.
jokes.setup: Shauna explains why she wants to write the bachelor party story
jokes.punchline: The joke is structural: this earnest journalistic mission statement is immediately undercut by Ben using it to set Shauna up with Chris — treating sincere values as a dating compatibility test
jokes.explanation: The comedic beat here is gentle — the joke is really in the setup for the Chris/Shauna setup rather than a strong punchline of its own. Works as warm character moment more than a laugh.

jokes.text: Are you a vegetarian? A vegan? A pescatarian? Not that it matters. / Um, I like burgers. / Perfect.
jokes.setup: Chris is asking Shauna to lunch; his anxious dietary question spiral suggests he's desperately hoping she'll fit into his health-conscious world
jokes.punchline: 'I like burgers' / 'Perfect.' — the new Chris (post character arc) has evolved enough to find burgers 'Perfect' rather than a cause for concern; the rapid relief in 'Perfect' is the joke
jokes.explanation: The joke works as character payoff for Chris's growth arc. The list of dietary restrictions — vegetarian, vegan, pescatarian — is classic Chris anxiety, but his 'Perfect' response to burgers shows he's evolved past his health obsession. 'Not that it matters' as a qualifier is a nice tell that he's trying not to be that person anymore. Good economy.

jokes.text: How great a day was today? Oh, God, I could die. Greatest day of my life. I met Andrew Luck today. I met Reggie Wayne today. And I met Jim Irsay. I'm standing on the field. Lucas Oil Stadium. And I'm playing football with my friends.
jokes.setup: The episode's closing sequence; Andy reflects on the day
jokes.punchline: Andy's complete, guileless joy — 'Oh, God, I could die' — treating a day of extraordinary celebrity access as the personal miracle it truly is for him; the comedy is in the wholeness of his happiness
jokes.explanation: The closing Andy speech is more heartwarming than comedic — it functions as an emotional button on the episode rather than a hard joke. 'Oh, God, I could die' is the funniest moment in it. The joke is in the simplicity of Andy's happiness inventory: famous people, famous field, his friends. Andy at his most affecting.

tmdb_overview: Ben and Leslie's rival bachelor and bachelorette parties each take on a very different tune.
insight: Two competing campaign events generate 72 jokes in 38 minutes—character comedy carries a borderline episode.
